scenes.vo: This is a school paddle. In Texas, it is still legal.

The school year was twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four. Texas public schools reported corporal punishment of five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine students. That is not a count of incidents. It is a count of children. Not in nineteen seventy-four. Last year.

Five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine students. Eight thousand, five hundred and twenty-eight separate instances, so many of them were struck more than once. In two hundred and eighty-four districts.

Texas law defines it plainly. Quote: the deliberate infliction of physical pain by hitting, paddling, spanking, slapping, or any other physical force used as a means of discipline. The law does not require it. It does not recommend it. It permits it, if a school board says so, unless a parent files a signed letter. Every year.

And here is the thing. It is already leaving. In twenty seventeen, Texas districts reported thirteen thousand, eight hundred and ninety-two students paddled. Four years later, seven thousand, three hundred and twenty-four. Last year, five thousand, three hundred and fifty-nine. Down sixty-one percent, with no change in the law. Principals and boards are quietly stopping on their own.

Who is it landing on? Of every one hundred students paddled in Texas, eighty-three are boys. Twenty-two have a disability. And nationally, the United States Secretary of Education told every governor that Black students are more than twice as likely to be paddled as white students, and Black girls four times as likely as white girls.

The paddle is meant to change behavior. A review of twenty-one studies, covering sixty-seven thousand, four hundred children, linked school corporal punishment to more aggression, more anxiety and depression, and lower school performance. The American Academy of Pediatrics calls physical punishment minimally effective in the short term and ineffective over time. Its recommendation for schools is plain: abolish it. The behavior the paddle is meant to stop is the behavior it most reliably produces.

overlays.text: More aggression. More anxiety. Lower grades.
American Academy of Pediatrics: abolish it

scenes.vo: For the adult holding it, the law offers protection, right up to three words. Excessive. Reasonable. Necessary. Texas shields a teacher from personal liability, except for excessive force. It shields their job and certificate, only for force a court later agrees was reasonable and necessary. Those words are decided afterward, by someone else, who will be shown the research.
Three hundred Texas school boards already prohibit corporal punishment in board policy. Two hundred and ninety-one of them use exactly the same sentence.
The Board prohibits the use of corporal punishment in the District. That is the whole policy. One sentence, in a policy code every Texas board already has.

Three hundred and ninety-six districts still permit it on paper, and did not use it once last year. For those boards, nothing changes on Monday morning except the risk. One sentence. One meeting. And the paddle comes off the wall for good.

overlays.text: 396 districts: permitted on paper, no reported use

scenes.vo: Find your district's policy, in its own words, at earthpilot dot org, slash kids. Bring the sentence to your board. The Safe Schools Project.
